question: How do I hire a fractional CRO for a logistics business?
body:
## Direct Answer
Hire a fractional CRO for a logistics business by scoping a 10-to-20-hour-per-week engagement, prioritizing candidates with freight, 3PL, or supply-chain revenue experience, and structuring a 90-day trial with defined pipeline, retention, and margin targets. Expect a monthly retainer rather than a full salary, and tie the contract to measurable revenue outcomes, not hours logged. The right operator fixes your commercial engine — pricing, sales coverage, and customer retention — without the cost of a permanent executive.

A fractional Chief Revenue Officer gives a logistics company senior commercial leadership for a fraction of a full-time hire's cost, which matters when freight margins are thin and a bad quarter erases a year of gains. The hard part is not finding someone with a CRO title — it is finding one who understands load boards, carrier relationships, brokerage spreads, contract-versus-spot dynamics, and the operational reality that a sales promise your operations team cannot deliver is worse than no sale at all. This guide walks through when to hire, how to source and vet candidates, what to pay, how to structure the engagement, and how to measure whether it is working.

## When does a logistics business actually need a fractional CRO instead of a VP of Sales?
The distinction matters more in logistics than in most industries because the revenue problem is rarely just "we need more salespeople." A VP of Sales manages reps and a quota. A CRO — fractional or not — owns the entire revenue system: pricing and rate strategy, sales, marketing, customer success, and the handoffs between them. In a freight brokerage or 3PL, revenue leaks happen at the seams — a shipper churns because service failed, a lane loses money because pricing never adjusted to a carrier-rate spike, a large account was never expanded beyond the one lane that won it. Those are CRO problems, not rep problems.

You need the fractional version specifically when the company is between roughly two and forty million dollars in revenue, or larger but structurally stuck, and cannot yet justify a $250K-plus base salary plus equity plus bonus for a full-time commercial chief. The fractional CRO is the right call when you have a real revenue architecture problem — misaligned pricing, no retention motion, a sales team selling on price alone — but not enough scale or complexity to keep a full-time executive busy and accountable five days a week. If your only problem is that you need more outbound activity, hire a sales manager and save the money. If your revenue engine itself is broken or was never built, that is the fractional CRO's job. For the broader build-versus-buy decision, see the framework at https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/revops-leadership-hire.

There is also a timing signal specific to logistics. Freight markets are cyclical — you will hit down-cycles where spot rates collapse and shippers renegotiate. A fractional CRO earns their retainer in exactly those moments by defending margin, re-segmenting the book, and protecting the accounts worth keeping while the market is ugly. Bringing one in *before* the cycle turns, not after you have already bled two quarters of margin, is the difference between a rescue and a rebuild.

## What logistics-specific experience should I demand from candidates?
Generic B2B SaaS revenue experience does not transfer cleanly to freight. The economics are different: gross margins in brokerage often run in the low double digits, cash cycles are brutal because you pay carriers before shippers pay you, and "the product" is a service delivered by third parties you do not control. A CRO who has only ever sold software with 80% gross margins will make pricing decisions that quietly destroy a brokerage. Demand direct experience in at least one adjacent lane: freight brokerage, asset-based carriers, 3PL or 4PL, warehousing and fulfillment, drayage, or LTL/FTL sales leadership.

Probe for specific fluency. Can the candidate talk credibly about contract versus spot mix and how they would shift it? Do they understand load-board dynamics and how carrier sales and shipper sales are two different motions that must be balanced? Have they managed the tension between a sales team that wants to win freight and an operations team that has to cover the loads profitably? Ask how they think about customer concentration risk — many logistics businesses have a terrifying share of revenue in their top three accounts, and a real CRO treats de-concentration as a strategic priority, not an afterthought.

The second demand is systems and data fluency. Modern logistics revenue leadership runs on a TMS (transportation management system) and increasingly on a CRM layered over it. A fractional CRO who cannot read a margin-by-lane report, cannot instrument a pipeline, and cannot connect quoting behavior to won-margin outcomes will manage on vibes. You want someone who will walk in, pull the data, and within weeks tell you which lanes and which customers actually make money — a surprising number of logistics operators do not know. The diagnostic-first approach is covered further at https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/revenue-diagnostic-90-day.

```mermaid
  B -->|Not enough activity| C[Hire a sales manager]
  B -->|System is broken| D[Hire a fractional CRO]
  D --> E[Pricing and rate strategy]
  D --> F[Sales coverage and comp]
  D --> G[Customer retention]
  D --> H[Margin by lane]
  E --> I[Defended and growing margin]
  F --> I
  G --> I

```

## Where do I find qualified fractional CRO candidates?
Sourcing a fractional executive is different from posting a job. The best candidates are rarely on job boards because they are running a portfolio of two to four clients and grow through referral. Start with the networks that concentrate operators: fractional-executive marketplaces and communities, logistics-specific groups on LinkedIn, freight and supply-chain associations, and your own investor or lender network — private equity and asset-based lenders who work with logistics companies see who turned a book around and who did not.

Referrals from other logistics founders are the single highest-signal channel. A fractional CRO who fixed a peer's margin problem comes with a reference already attached. Second, look at people who recently exited or sold a logistics company and are not ready to fully retire — they have operator scars and time. Third, consider recruiters who specialize in fractional and interim executive placement, though you pay a premium and should still run your own vetting. Avoid the trap of hiring a generic "fractional CRO" personality who has a slick deck but has never covered a load or defended a lane rate in a down market.

When you build a shortlist, weight it toward operators over consultants. A consultant produces a strategy document; a fractional CRO produces changed behavior and changed numbers. In logistics, where execution and relationships drive everything, you want the person who will get on the phone with your biggest shipper, not the one who will present findings and leave. The vendor-and-network sourcing map is expanded at https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/fractional-executive-sourcing.

## How do I structure and price the engagement?
Fractional CRO engagements are almost always retainer-based, priced on a monthly fee for a defined time commitment rather than an hourly rate or a full salary. The commitment typically ranges from one to three days per week, or roughly 10 to 30 hours. Pricing varies widely by market, experience, and scope, so do not anchor on a single number — instead, structure the deal so cost scales with value and risk is shared.

Structure it in three layers. First, a base retainer that covers the committed hours and guarantees you priority access. Second, a variable or success component tied to outcomes you both agree are the point of the engagement — new margin dollars, retention improvement, a repriced book, a built and staffed sales function. Third, a defined term with a real off-ramp: a 90-day initial period that either converts to an ongoing engagement or ends cleanly. Avoid open-ended retainers with no success metric; they drift into expensive advisory relationships that never move the number.

Be honest about the ramp. A fractional CRO cannot fix a broken revenue engine in 30 days, but they should produce a diagnosis and a prioritized plan in the first 30, visible motion by 60, and early results by 90. Build the payment cadence to match — front-loaded enough that a strong operator will take the engagement, but structured so you are not paying full freight for a relationship that is not producing by month three. Do not misclassify this as a pure cost decision. A CRO who defends two points of margin on a book doing meaningful volume pays for themselves many times over, and the retainer is trivial against that. For comp benchmarking methodology, see https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/fractional-comp-benchmarks.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A[Day 0 kickoff] --> B[Days 1 to 30 diagnose]
  B --> C[Days 31 to 60 build and reprice]
  C --> D[Days 61 to 90 early results]
  D --> E{Decision}
  E -->|Working| F[Convert to ongoing]
  E -->|Not working| G[Clean off ramp]
```

## What does the first 90 days look like, and how do I measure success?
The engagement should open with a diagnosis, not a plan. In the first two to four weeks the fractional CRO pulls the data — margin by lane, margin by customer, sales pipeline, quote-to-book conversion, customer concentration, churn and retention, and the comp plan driving rep behavior. In logistics this almost always surfaces uncomfortable truths: a chunk of the book is unprofitable, pricing has not kept pace with carrier costs, the top few accounts carry dangerous concentration, and reps are compensated on revenue rather than margin, so they chase bad freight. Getting these truths on the table is the first deliverable.

From there, define three to five outcomes and instrument them from day one. Good logistics CRO metrics include gross margin percentage and gross margin dollars (not just top-line revenue, which lies in freight), net revenue retention on the shipper book, customer concentration ratio, sales cycle and quote-to-book conversion, and pipeline coverage against target. Set a baseline in week one and review against it monthly. If the CRO cannot show you a baseline and a trend line, the engagement is not being run correctly.

Measure the operator on behavior change as well as numbers, because numbers lag. Did they rebuild the comp plan to reward margin? Did they re-segment the book and put a retention motion on the accounts worth keeping? Did they install a pricing discipline so lane rates adjust to carrier-cost moves instead of eroding silently? Did they hire, coach, or replace the right people? These leading indicators tell you at day 60 whether the day-120 numbers will move. The decision at the end of the initial term is binary and unsentimental: the trajectory is either bending the right way or it is not. Hold the line on that review — the discipline of the checkpoint is what separates a fractional hire from an expensive open-ended advisor. The full scorecard template lives at https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/cro-scorecard-logistics.

## What are the biggest mistakes logistics owners make with this hire?
The first mistake is hiring for the title instead of the outcome. A fractional CRO is not a status symbol; it is a specific intervention on a specific revenue problem. If you cannot articulate the problem in one sentence — "our margins are eroding and no one owns pricing," or "we grew on one big account and have to diversify before it walks" — you are not ready to hire, and any candidate will happily take your retainer while the problem stays fuzzy.

The second mistake is under-empowering the person. A fractional CRO who cannot change the comp plan, cannot reprice lanes, cannot hire or move people, and cannot get on the phone with your top customers is a consultant with a fancier title. Give real authority within a defined scope, or do not bother. In a founder-led logistics business this is genuinely hard, because the founder usually *is* the revenue engine and handing over the commercial keys feels like losing control. Name that tension out loud in the contract and agree on the decision rights up front.

The third mistake is impatience with the wrong things and patience with the right things. Owners often panic when new revenue does not appear in month one — but the first job is usually to *stop the bleeding* on margin, which does not show as top-line growth and sometimes looks like walking away from bad freight and shrinking revenue on purpose. Conversely, owners are too patient with an operator who at day 60 has produced a deck but no changed behavior. Invert that: be patient while margin repair works its way through, and impatient about the absence of visible operational change. A wrong-market hire — a SaaS revenue leader in a freight business — is the classic version of both mistakes at once.

## Related questions

### How much does a fractional CRO cost compared to a full-time hire?
A fractional CRO is a monthly retainer for part-time commitment rather than a full base salary plus bonus and equity. The exact figure depends on market, experience, and hours, but the whole point is senior leadership at a fraction of full-time cost — and it should be justified by margin defended, not hours logged.

### Can one fractional CRO cover both sales and operations in logistics?
No. A CRO owns the commercial engine — pricing, sales, retention, marketing. Operations (load coverage, carrier management, service delivery) needs its own leader. The CRO's job is to align commercial promises with operational reality, not to run dispatch.

### How long should a fractional CRO engagement last?
Structure an initial 90-day term with a clear decision point, then convert to an ongoing monthly engagement if the trajectory is working. Many logistics engagements run six to eighteen months — long enough to rebuild the revenue system, then taper as internal leadership takes over.

### Should I hire fractional or just promote my best salesperson?
Your best salesperson is usually your best *seller*, not your best *revenue architect*. Promoting them often loses your top producer and gains a mediocre executive. A fractional CRO can build the system and coach that person into a real leadership role — keeping their selling strength intact.

### What is the difference between a fractional CRO and a sales consultant?
A consultant produces analysis and a strategy document, then leaves. A fractional CRO owns the outcome, holds authority to change comp, pricing, and staffing, and stays embedded until the numbers move. In logistics, where execution beats slideware, that ownership is the whole value.

## FAQ

**Do I need a fractional CRO if I already have a VP of Sales?**
Possibly. A VP of Sales manages reps and quota; a CRO owns the whole revenue system including pricing, retention, and margin. If your VP is executing well but the revenue *architecture* is broken, a fractional CRO can build the system above them. If the VP is underperforming at their own job, fix that first.

**How many hours per week does a fractional CRO work?**
Typically one to three days, roughly 10 to 30 hours, depending on scope and stage. The commitment should be defined in the contract with guaranteed priority access, not billed hourly. If the problem is large, you can scale hours up during the intensive build phase and taper later.

**What size logistics company is right for a fractional CRO?**
Roughly two to forty million in revenue is the sweet spot — large enough to have a real revenue engine worth fixing, small enough that a full-time CRO is not yet justified. Larger companies use fractional CROs for turnarounds, carve-outs, or interim coverage during a search.

**Will a fractional CRO understand my freight or 3PL business?**
Only if you demand relevant experience. Insist on direct freight, brokerage, 3PL, warehousing, or supply-chain background. A generic B2B or SaaS revenue leader will misprice a thin-margin freight book. Vet for fluency in contract-versus-spot dynamics, carrier relationships, and margin-by-lane thinking.

**How do I measure whether the engagement is working?**
Baseline three to five metrics in week one — gross margin dollars and percent, net revenue retention, customer concentration, quote-to-book conversion, pipeline coverage — and review monthly. Also track behavior change: repriced lanes, a margin-based comp plan, a retention motion. Numbers lag; changed behavior at day 60 predicts results at day 120.

**Can a fractional CRO become full-time later?**
Yes, and it is a common and healthy path. The fractional engagement is effectively a long working interview for both sides. If the operator fits the culture and the business grows enough to justify a full-time commercial chief, converting is lower-risk than hiring cold. Build an optional conversion path into the initial contract.

**What happens to the work when the engagement ends?**
A good fractional CRO builds systems and people that outlast them — a documented pricing discipline, an instrumented pipeline, a coached internal leader, a rebuilt comp plan. If the engagement ends and everything reverts, the CRO ran it as advisory instead of building durable capability. Require a handoff plan as an explicit deliverable.

**Should the fractional CRO have equity?**
Sometimes, for longer engagements where you want deep alignment, a small equity or profit-share component can supplement the retainer. For short 90-day interventions, a cash retainer with a success bonus is usually cleaner. Match the structure to the term and the outcome you are buying.
